plan.topic: Orforglipron (Foundayo), the once-daily GLP-1 pill approved in the US for chronic weight management: what to expect when you start. A fresh 9-minute script written only from the US prescribing information (rev 7/2026) and the Medication Guide, replacing the parked script (5 failures). The parked script is not re-rendered.
plan.angle:
Keep the brief's structure, with these changes:
- Opening: 'If you're starting orforglipron, the Foundayo pill, the label says nausea is the most likely thing you'll notice. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher during the dosage escalation period and decreased over time.'
- 15–30 s: −11.1% vs placebo at the highest label dose in Trial 1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes).
- Chapter 2: nausea about 35 in 100 vs 10 in 100 on placebo at the highest label dose. Stopping because of adverse events: 10 in 100 at the highest label dose vs 3 in 100 on placebo. Card scope for both: 'pooled Trials 1 and 2: adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition, with or without type 2 diabetes'. Drop 10.3% vs 2.7% entirely.
- Chapter 1: 'once daily, with or without food; swallow tablets whole'. Add 'any time of day' only if found in the PI.
- Chapter 4 pancreatitis: 'Stop taking FOUNDAYO and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting.'
- NAION: the FDA's 9 Nov 2026 Drug Safety Communication on a 'potential' risk, sourced to the FDA page.
- Everything else as briefed.
plan.working_title: Orforglipron (Foundayo) Pill: What Happens When You Start?
plan.why:
Playbook queue #1 and our strongest signal: drug-name search (the old Foundayo video adds about 60 min a day) plus Foundayo Shorts at 833 and 896 views. The parked script failed 5 times, so this is a fresh script built on the label. | fact-check: The topic is sound and on-pillar. Orforglipron (Foundayo) is FDA-approved and the US PI (rev July 2026) is live at https://uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html. I checked the brief against that PI and found five problems.
(1) The stopping figure in the brief is wrong. 10.3% vs 2.7% is the trial-only 36 mg arm. The label (6.1) says: '8% of patients treated with FOUNDAYO (5.5 mg, 6%; 9 mg, 9%; and 17.2 mg, 10%) … permanently discontinued treatment as a result of adverse reactions compared to 3% of patients receiving placebo.' The 6.1 pool is Trials 1 AND 2, and Trial 2 enrolled adults WITH type 2 diabetes. So the stopping and symptom stats must never be scoped as 'without diabetes' or as 'Trial 1'.
(2) The example opening sentence uses 'mostly', which the brief itself bans. The label says: 'The incidence of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea was higher during the FOUNDAYO dosage escalation period and decreased over time.'
(3) The Medication Guide's pancreatitis action is 'Stop taking FOUNDAYO and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting.' 'Get medical help right away' is NOT the pancreatitis wording, so don't carry it over from the parked fixes for this line.
(4) Section 2, as I found it, says 'once daily, with or without food' and 'swallow tablets whole. Do not break, crush, or chew.' I could not confirm 'at any time of day'. Use it only if the scriptwriter finds that sentence in the PI.
(5) NAION is not in section 5 of the July 2026 PI. Credit it to the FDA Drug Safety Communication of 9 Nov 2026 (orforglipron is named in it), keep the word 'potential', and source it to the FDA DSC page, not a news article.
The −11.1% for the highest label dose in Trial 1 stays as briefed (its population excluded diabetes). Nausea at the highest label dose is 35% vs 10% on placebo, in the pooled Trials 1 and 2. Headache, fatigue and hair loss are confirmed on the common list.

package.description:
Stop taking Foundayo and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

Quick answer: the US label for orforglipron (Foundayo) lists nausea as the most common adverse reaction. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher during dosage escalation and decreased over time. Trial 1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes): 11.1% average weight loss at the label's highest dose at 72 weeks vs 2.1% on placebo. Pooled Trials 1 and 2 (same groups, with or without type 2 diabetes), highest dose: nausea about 35 vs 10 in 100 on placebo; 10 vs 3 in 100 permanently stopped treatment because of adverse reactions.

Sources:
1. Foundayo US Prescribing Information and Medication Guide, rev 7/2026: https://uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html
2. NHS, Feeling sick (nausea), reviewed 17 Nov 2023: https://www.nhs.uk/symptoms/feeling-sick-nausea/

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary: I checked every number, quote and patient group against the FOUNDAYO label (prescribing information plus Medication Guide, rev 7/2026), the FDA eye-safety notice of 9 Nov 2026 and the NHS nausea page (reviewed 17 Nov 2023), and all of them match. Weight result: Trial 1 at 17.2 mg, −11.1% vs −2.1% on placebo at 72 weeks; the label says people with type 2 diabetes were excluded. Pooled Trials 1 and 2 (3,155 adults, 31% with type 2 diabetes): nausea 35% vs 10%, and stopping because of adverse reactions 10% at the top dose and 8% across all doses vs 3% on placebo. The escalation sentence and the pancreatitis line ('with or without nausea or vomiting') match the label word for word. Headache, fatigue and hair loss are on the label's common list. What it's approved for and how to take it (once daily, with or without food, swallowed whole) match sections 1 and 2. The FDA notice names Foundayo (orforglipron), keeps the word 'potential', describes reduced blood flow to the optic nerve and vision loss, and tells patients to contact their provider right away. Every NHS tip is on the NHS page. All required safety lines are present, there are no dose numbers, and Priya is clearly hypothetical. One minor fix: remove the NHS source tag from s35, which mixes in our own tips. The Medication Guide is printed on the same Lilly page as the prescribing information and has no URL of its own, so citing that one URL is acceptable.

NORMAL?') pairs a specific, relatable new-starter worry with a facial expression (anxious/queasy stomach) that matches the emotional tone of the text exactly, creating a strong curiosity gap without resolving it — it asks a question tied directly to the title's 'what to expect when you start' intent, and the channel's data cites this exact pattern at 4.13% CTR. #1's big stat ('-11.1%') is compelling but is a weight-loss trial figure, somewhat orthogonal to the title's focus on the starting/early-days experience, and its subtext wraps awkwardly in the small crop. #2's giant question mark is pure mystery with no emotional anchor (no face), typically a slightly weaker pull than a relatable human/body reaction for this audience. None of the candidates give away the answer or show a text/emotion mismatch, so #0 wins on expected CTR while keeping full legibility.
